{{Short description|1665 work by Athanasius Kircher}}
{{italic title}}
[[File:Arithmologia sive De abditis numerorum mysterijs.png|thumb|Title page of ''Arithmologia sive De abditis numerorum mysterijs'']]
[[File:Illustration from Kircher’s “Arithmologia”.jpg|thumb|Illustration from Kircher’s “Arithmologia”]]
[[File:Arithmologia, engraved titlepage. Wellcome L0016023.jpg|thumb|Frontispiece of ''Arithmologia'']]
'''''Arithmologia, sive De Abditis Numerorum Mysteriis''''' is a 1665 work by the [[Jesuit]] scholar [[Athanasius Kircher]]. It was published by Varese, the main printing house for the Jesuit order in Rome in the mid-17th century.<ref>{{cite web |title='Athanasii Kircheri ... Arithmologia, sive de Abditis numerorum mysteriis.' |url=https://www.worldcat.org/formats-editions/778034604 |website=worldcat.org |accessdate=21 June 2020}}</ref><ref name="Kendrick2018">{{cite book|author=Robert L. Kendrick|title=Fruits of the Cross: Passiontide Music Theater in Habsburg Vienna|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=cdVwDwAAQBAJ&pg=PA36|accessdate=21 June 2020|date=13 November 2018|publisher=Univ of California Press|isbn=978-0-520-29757-9|pages=36–}}</ref> It was dedicated to [[Franz III. Nádasdy]],<ref name="Library2003">{{cite book|author=Harold B. Lee Library|title=Athanasius Kircher (1602-1680), Jesuit Scholar: An Exhibition of His Works in the Harold B. Lee Library Collections at Brigham Young University|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=29984eQF86UC&pg=PA44|accessdate=21 June 2020|year=2003|publisher=Martino Publishing|isbn=978-1-57898-432-9|pages=44–6}}</ref> a convert to Catholicism to whom Kircher had previously co-dedicated ''[[Oedipus Aegyptiacus]]''.<ref name="AlmásiBrzeziński2015">{{cite book|author1=Gábor Almási|author2=Szymon Brzeziński|author3=Ildikó Horn|title=A Divided Hungary in Europe: Exchanges, Networks and Representations, 1541-1699; Volume 1 – Study Tours and Intellectual-Religious Relationships|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=7u-mBgAAQBAJ&pg=PA164|date=12 January 2015|publisher=Cambridge Scholars Publishing|isbn=978-1-4438-7294-2|pages=164–}}</ref> ''Arithmologia'' is the only one of Kircher's works devoted entirely to different aspects of number symbolism.<ref name="LawrenceMcCartney2015">{{cite book|author1=Snezana Lawrence|author1-link= Snezana Lawrence |author2=Mark McCartney|title=Mathematicians and their Gods: Interactions between mathematics and religious beliefs|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=bO2kCQAAQBAJ&pg=PA293|accessdate=21 June 2020|date=23 July 2015|publisher=OUP Oxford|isbn=978-0-19-100754-5|pages=113–4}}</ref>

==Content==
''Arithmologia'' was concerned with exploring numbers as the underlying principle and structure of the universe, and as the key to mystic understanding previously revealed to patriarchs and philosophers in ancient times. The field of arithmology may be understood as the intersection of traditional religious numerology and contemporary mathematics, drawing on ideas from [[Pythagoras#Numerology|Pythagoras]], [[Gnosticism]], and the [[Kabbalah|Kabbala]]. The work discussed the significance of numbers in astrology, divination, magic formulas, amulets, seals and symbolic matrices.<ref name="Library2003"/><ref name="Eco2014">{{cite book|author=Umberto Eco|title=From the Tree to the Labyrinth|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=nh35AgAAQBAJ&pg=PA614|accessdate=21 June 2020|date=25 February 2014|publisher=Harvard University Press|isbn=978-0-674-72816-5|page=614}}</ref> Kircher's purpose, as he declared in the final chapter, was to articulate a Christian philosophy of number, revealing the hidden harmonies within the material world and its connections with the spiritual.<ref name="LawrenceMcCartney2015"/>

==Illustrations==
The frontispiece depicts, at the top, the all-seeing [[Eye of Providence]] within a triangle representing the [[Holy Trinity]]. In each angle Hebrew letters spell out [[Jah]], the name of God. Around this the nine [[Hierarchy of angels|orders of angels]] are arranged in three more overlapping triangles. Beneath this fly two [[putto|putti]], one carrying a ruler and a [[plumb line]], while the other carries a tablet with the magic square of three. Within this square, numbers can be added by row, by column or diagonally, but always add up to fifteen.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Beinlich |first1=H.C. |last2=Daxelmüller |first2=H.J. |last3=Vollrath |first3=K. |title=Kircher und die Mathematik in "Magie des Wissens" |url=http://www.history.didaktik.mathematik.uni-wuerzburg.de/vollrath/papers/087.pdf |website=uni.wuerzberg.de |publisher=University of Würzberg |accessdate=21 June 2020}}</ref> This figure can be compared similarly to that of the enneagram.<ref>{{Cite web |title=The Enneagram |url=https://gurdjiefflegacy.org/70links/enneagram.htm}}</ref>

In the centre of the image is a winged representation of the cosmos; the winged sphere was an ancient Egyptian symbol that Kircher interpreted as meaning the ''[[anima mundi]]''. On the outer rim of this sphere are the [[Primum Mobile|primum mobile]] and the fixed stars, and within them the planets orbiting around the static earth at the centre. Beneath this, in the realm of the physical world, sit a learned Jew with an open book displaying the stars of David and Solomon, and a classical philosopher pointing to a model of [[Pythagoras' theorem]].<ref name="Godwin">{{cite book |last1=Godwin |first1=Joscelyn |title=Athanasius Kircher's Theatre of the World |date=2015 |publisher=Inner Traditions |location=Rochester, Vermont |isbn=978-1-62055-465-4}}</ref>{{rp|34}}
